chapter_theme: Natrinai 81 to 100: returns and promised seasons kept or mistaken (the soldier racing home to a wife who longs to host guests, the friend who praises one man's punctuality and mocks the flowers that bloom for another's absence), hill trysts at night with owl, boar and elephant as the night's dangers, shore poems of memory and pallor pressing for marriage, a woman who resents that only men may speak their love, and marutham scenes of a poor girl at a festival swing and a courtesan laughing at a husband afraid of his wife.

81.reading: Back from the king's war, the man tells his charioteer to yoke the chariot whose swift horses, prized by kings, have bells ringing on their clipped-mane necks: the strong-sworded king has quelled the enemy, and they will see the sweet smile of the lovely young wife who has stayed weeping, tears dropping on her breasts, worn out by her longing to welcome guests.
81.nuance: Her grief is named as a thwarted wish to host guests (விருந்து அயர் விருப்பு), a duty a wife cannot keep alone, so his return restores the household's work as well as the marriage. The king's victory is held back to the last line, as the thing that releases him.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றிய தலைவன்தேர்ப்பாகற்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the wife waiting at home and the husband freed by the war's end is the mullai situation

82.reading: The man asks the hill girl of graceful gait, whose bamboo-lovely shoulders could end his sickness and weakness, whether she knows his anguish: he cannot bear to look at her form, which strikes the eyes like Valli joined with Murugan, she of the small village where hunters carry home the spoil their dogs took when they broke the leash and swarmed an angry boar, its dark mud-bathed back mingled with dust, at the forked path where snakes go.
82.nuance: Line 1 credits her shoulders with ending the very sickness she causes. The closing scene of dogs swarming a proud boar while the hunters take the spoil can be read as the man brought down by her, but no second correspondence is anchored in the poem, so the boar stays scene (a near miss for ullurai). Line 7 recurs as Natrinai 386 line 1.

colophon.thurai: தோழியிற்புணர்ச்சிக்கண் தன்னிலைக் கொளீஇயது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill girl, the boar and the hunters are kurinji things

comparisons.tenor: the girl's form that dazzles his eyes

83.reading: The friend promises the owl that has long lived in the old god-haunted tree at the drinking ghat by their town's gate, sharp of claw and curved of beak, a rich feast of white rice cooked in ghee with dark meat and roasted white rat, if only it will not keep sounding its harsh, fearful cry in the hour when they lie awake and restless, longing for the coming of their lover of unfailing resolve.
83.nuance: The plea to the owl is meant for the man waiting outside: it tells him they are awake and waiting, and that the meeting depends on the house not being roused. Rice, ghee and meat are the stuff of offerings at a god's tree, so the friend is bribing an omen.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைவன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாக தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: lying awake for the lover's coming is the night tryst of kurinji

84.reading: The woman tells her friend that only yesterday he was here, praising her eyes, her shoulders, her cool fragrant hair and her speckled waist, and today they say he will go by the hard road where the sun sits enthroned, through omai forest on salt waste cracked like unformed butter split by heat, where the white ghost-chariot of the mirage, like a great water, lures the deer across the long treeless stretch: he is one who cannot live a home life that fails to relieve those who come to beg.
84.nuance: The last lines give his reason without blame: a household that cannot relieve suppliants is no life for him, so the ideal of giving is what takes him from her. ஏகுவர் என்ப (they say he will go) shows she has the news from others, not from him, and the colophon's 'in separation' anticipates a parting not yet made.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை ஆற்றாளாய தலைவி தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: his going over the waste is the paalai parting

comparisons.vehicle: சுடுமண் தசும்பின் மத்தம் தின்ற பிறவா வெண்ணெய் உருப்பு இடந்தன்ன

85.reading: The friend tells the woman that though her fine flower eyes drip tears, her bangles slip from her bamboo-like shoulders and the gossiping old town is loud, she wishes the lord of the high mountain would not come for love of her by the narrow, fearful path black with night, where an elephant, afraid of the small-striped tiger, stands guarding its short-stepping calf: his is the land where the hill girl with honey-scented hair shares out, with tubers, in their kaanthal hamlet, the fat cut of the porcupine her hunter shot.
85.nuance: வாரற்கதில்ல (may he not come) is a wish against the woman's own longing, made from fear for him. The closing picture of the hunter's kill shared out in the hamlet sets the safe daylight order of a married hill household against the night path.

colophon.thurai: தலைவன் வரவு உணர்ந்த தோழி தலைவிக்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain and the dark night fix kurinji

iraicchi.act: the elephant, afraid of the tiger, halts on the dark path and stands guard over its short-stepping calf
iraicchi.sense: as the elephant keeps its young from the path's danger, the women's love for the man makes them wish him kept from that path at night, so love here means holding back, not coming

86.reading: The friend blesses the men as righteous: through the harsh dew of the late cold season, when the pakandrai blooms like leather cups and the great closed buds of the koongam open curled like a skilled craftsman's stitched work, they came back ahead of the early summer, when the eengai's good shoots sway, before the time they had named.
86.nuance: அறவர் (they are righteous) is praise for a kept promise, not for piety: keeping the season they named is what makes the man good. The flowers of the late dew and the not-yet-ripe summer fix that he beat his own deadline.

colophon.thurai: குறித்த பருவத்தின்வினைமுடித்து வந்தமை கேட்ட தோழி தலைவிக்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the late dew and the early summer are seasons Tholkappiyam gives to paalai

comparisons.tenor: a spreading part of the flowering plant

comparisons.vehicle: கை வல் வினைவன் தையுபு சொரிந்த சுரிதக உருவின

87.reading: The woman tells her friend that the day she spent thinking of the joys of the fisherfolk of his small village, where the dew-broken buds of the great punnai drip on the wet backs of oysters grazing at the shore, and of his great cool grove, has passed like the dream that a sharp-toothed bat, hanging asleep on a high mango branch in the town, dreams of the sour taste of gooseberries in Azhisi's great forest in the land of the war-winning Cholas.
87.nuance: The bat on the town's mango dreams of fruit in a far forest it is not in, as she dwells on a shore she has not reached: the simile makes her day of longing as unreal and as hungry as the bat's dream. The colophon says she saw a dream; the poem gives the dream to the bat and calls her own state remembering (நினைந்த).

colophon.thurai: வரைவிடை வைத்துப்பிரிய ஆற்றாளாய தலைவி கனாக் கண்டு தோழிக்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove and the fisherfolk fix neythal

comparisons.tenor: her day of longing for his shore

88.reading: The friend tells the woman not to be stricken as though by old deeds of their own, not to grieve, but to rise so they can go, speak to him and come back; she fears the woman will melt away like the sea-grown salt that has taken the rain, and, look, his hill heavy with ripe fruit, taking his cruelty to them to heart and too kind to bear it, will weep with waterfalls for tears.
88.nuance: The friend refuses fate (யாம் செய் தொல் வினை) as an explanation and proposes to act, and says it for the ears of the man outside: his own hill is shown weeping at his cruelty, so the land shames its lord. The salt of the shore, called the sea's nectar, is a neythal thing used in a hill poem.

colophon.thurai: சிறைப்புறமாகத்தோழி தலைவிக்கு உரைப்பாளாய்ச்சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: his fruit-laden hill and its falls fix kurinji

89.reading: As the great full-bellied clouds that rose in ranks like the spray of waves have spent their last torrents and the season of heavy dew comes, the ungracious north wind, which every night tosses wide the broad leaves of the hairy-podded black gram, sighing like a caparisoned elephant, will come again, friend, with the sorrowful evening and loneliness before it, joined with the hard-hearted ones who do not come.
89.nuance: The wind and the evening are made allies of the absent men (வன்கணாளரோடு இயைந்த), so the season does his cruelty for him. The colophon gives the poem to the friend, who has heard he is coming back with wealth, but the address தோழி and 'the ones who do not come' read more naturally as the woman's own complaint.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் முற்றி மறுத்தந்தான் எனக் கேட்ட தோழி தலைவிக்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: waiting through the evening for one who has not come is the mullai situation

90.reading: In the old town loud with its dancing festival, the young daughter of a poor woman, with few bangles and lovely sparse hair, dressed in a flowered cloth that the tireless washerwoman, who never rests her hands for her many clients, had washed by night, ran up with an unfading garland swinging, but would not ride the great palmyra-rope swing though her bright-eyed companions urged her, and went away weeping; this king's assembly, keeping company with graceless men who would not end the quarrel over the swing, is of no use.
90.nuance: The poem says only that a poor girl lost her turn at the festival swing and that the court did nothing; said within the panan's hearing, it seems to set the wife, pushed aside in her own town while those who should judge look on, beside the girl. As ullurai it fails condition 1: the vehicle is a person and a court, not a native thing, so the hidden comparison is left to this note. The night-washed cloth and the unfading garland may mark her finery as borrowed.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகளுக்கு உரைப்பாளாய் பாணனை நெருங்கி வாயில்மறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the festival in the old town is the marutham world

91.reading: The friend tells the woman she must have sensed it: so that their small village may shine with a great, unstinting joy of giving, the long-shored lord's tall chariot, yoked to swift horses whose bells cry out like whirling birds, comes here by day, to the shore garden where the large-legged heron, searching the roaring cold sea with its mate under the high bank of flower-shedding punnai, drops red-edged little fish into the mouths of its calling young in the nest atop the branch.
91.nuance: Coming by day (பகல் இவண் வரவே) means coming openly, to ask for her in marriage; the giving that will make the village shine is the wedding's bounty.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகட்கு வரைவு மலிந்து உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord and the shore garden fix neythal

comparisons.tenor: the ringing of the horses' bells

iraicchi.act: the heron searches the sea together with its mate and drops the fish it catches into the mouths of its young in the nest
iraicchi.sense: the man who now comes openly will keep a house as the heron does, seeking with his wife and feeding their own

92.reading: The friend asks whether they will not think of us, the men who crossed the waste where a summer chameleon with its mate and a slow-gaited snake shrivel among the striped maral, and where, on the summit of a drought-held hill by the wide well of a hunters' hamlet, a killing tusker, warding off the bowmen, lets its young she-elephant and her calf drink from the gem-clear trough drawn for the cattle, and then goes its way.
92.nuance: The question expects yes: what the man saw on the road, a male winning water for its mate and calf and then leaving, is what he himself is doing, so the friend makes the road remind him.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட கிழத்திக்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: summer, drought and the waste fix paalai

iraicchi.act: the tusker wards off the bowmen so its mate and calf can drink at the hamlet's trough, and then goes on
iraicchi.sense: the man who crossed that land, seeing a male provide for its own and move on as he did, will think of the wife he left

93.reading: The friend tells the lord of the great rock land, where those who leave lament that this hill-crowned mountain, its honeycombs hanging, its great fruits clustered, its white falls coming down like garlands and all its grains spilling, is rich every day, to rise and come, long life to him: the soft young girl, slender-waisted, with jewels on bamboo shoulders that hide her sides, has the old pallor of one worn by shame, and her life, given like a pledge, is hard to win even for kings whose hairy-eyed drums thunder.
93.nuance: குறியெதிர்ப்பை is a loan repaid in kind: her life is given to him as such a loan, one even kings could not obtain, so his delay wastes what kings could not buy. The opening praise of a land so rich that leavers weep hints that he too should not leave her.

colophon.thurai: வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: the rock land and the mountain fix kurinji

94.reading: The woman tells her friend that when love-sickness tosses one and desire breaks composure, speaking out one's longing suits a man, while she must hold it in finely as womanhood restrains her; what kind of man is the lord of the fish-smelling shore, where punnai buds cluster like fresh pearls a skilled craftsman has not yet washed to beauty, that he does not know those who long for him and are tormented by his chest?
94.nuance: Said for the man outside to hear: she states the rule that only a man may speak his love and turns it into a reproach, since he, who may speak, does not. The pearls still unwashed, lovely but not yet brought out, are the shore's own figure for a love kept unspoken.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன்சிறைப்புறமாக தலைவி தோழிக்கு உரைப்பாளாய்ச்சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the fish-smelling shore and the punnai fix neythal

comparisons.vehicle: கை வல் கம்மியன் கவின் பெறக் கழாஅ மண்ணாப் பசு முத்து

95.reading: The man tells his companion where his heart is: on the hill where, while the bamboo pole hums and many instruments sound, the strong cub of a fluffy-headed monkey, red-faced like a sweet fig, swings on the strong twisted rope a dancing girl walked, then climbs the great rock by the bamboo and leaps up while the hill children clap time, there is a small hamlet ringed with thickets; in that hamlet is the hill girl of fragrant hair; and in her hand is his heart, bound so that no one else can free it.
95.nuance: The poem narrows like a chain, each phrase's last word starting the next (சீறூர், சீறூரோளே; கொடிச்சி, கொடிச்சி), from hill to hamlet to girl to her hand. The monkey cub playing on the dancer's rope while children clap is the place's ease, offered to the companion as directions.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பாங்கற்கு இவ்விடத்து இத்தன்மைத்து என உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill girl, the monkey and the hill people's children are kurinji things

96.reading: The friend points out to the woman the grove on one side of the white sand, crowded with punnai and strewn with the gnaazhal's fragrant flowers, where she newly joined him; the shore where the swelling waves played with them and he kindly dried the dark five-braided hair that hung down her back; and the shore garden where she went alone wearing a leaf dress woven of the long-stalked neythal of the curving backwater: thinking of them again and again she melts, and slowly the pallor has spread over her.
96.nuance: இதுவே, உதுவே, அதுவே point to this place, that one and the one further off, so the friend walks the overhearing man back through his own meeting places; ending on the pallor, which she addresses directly, she tells him the memories have become a sickness only marriage will cure. Line 8 recurs as Natrinai 123 line 7.

colophon.thurai: சிறைப்புறமாகத்தோழி தலைவிக்கு உரைப்பாளாய் வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater, the shore and the shore garden fix neythal

97.reading: The woman says that crueler than the koel, which cries out lonely though it is not parted, as cruel as a spear thrust into an aching heart whose deep wound's pus has not dried, is the river of clear water, and crueler still is the lone young daughter of the grove's farmers who wanders with a bee-circled basket calling, 'Won't you take mixed flowers of pitthikai and fresh kurukkatthi with fluffy-tipped petals?'
97.nuance: Each thing is crueler for being more ordinary: a bird's cry, then the river, then a farm girl selling flowers that a wife with her husband away will not wear, so the climax is a human voice selling the season. The koel is cruel because it laments without having been parted (பிரிவில புலம்பி). The colophon's mullai rests on the waiting; the season the poem names is spring.

colophon.thurai: பருவம் கண்டு ஆற்றாளாய தலைவி தோழிக்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the koel and the kurukkatthi mark spring, the season Tholkappiyam gives to paalai

98.reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where a small-eyed boar with coarse neck bristles like porcupine quills, coming to wallow in the wide millet field of the high mountain, is about to pass the gap where a heavy trap is set when a lizard chirps beside it, and at once backs away, slowly, slowly, to rest in its rock-cave bed: crueler even than his coming by night, watching for a lapse of the sleepless guards of her father's well-guarded wide house, is her own feckless heart, which will not keep company with eyes that cannot close any night.
98.nuance: The boar heeds a lizard's chirp and turns back from the trap; the man ignores the guards and keeps coming. 'My heart' may be the friend speaking in the girl's person: her heart goes out to him at night while her eyes stay awake, so the danger is now inside the house as well.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்து ஒழுகும்தலைவனைத் தோழி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: the high mountain and the night visit fix kurinji

ullurai.tenor: the man who comes to the guarded house by night

pairs.situation: he slips into the father's guarded house at the guards' lapse
the signs of danger that should warn him

pairs.scene: மெல்லமெல்லப் பிறக்கே பெயர்ந்து தன் கல் அளைப் பள்ளி வதியும்
pairs.situation: he should turn back from night visits and rest in a home of his own by marrying her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a boar of the hill's own millet field in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

99.reading: The friend answers the young woman who asked whether this is the season the men promised when they crossed the hot waste, its long way waterless, its heat shimmering like spread cloth: the great full-bellied cloud, mindless and forgetting itself, scooped up the sea and, unable to bear the load, let fall a heavy rain, and the pidavam, the konrai and the kodal, taking it for the rains with minds that cannot tell, have bloomed in numbers, because they are foolish.
99.nuance: The friend does not deny that it rains; she denies that the rain means anything, by making both the cloud (மதி இன்று, மறந்து) and the flowers (மடவ) mistaken. Laughing at the flowers' folly lets the woman laugh at her own fear. The flowers mistake a sign as she did, so they are the poem's subject, not iraicchi.

colophon.thurai: பருவம் கண்டு ஆற்றாளாய தலைவியைத் தோழி பருவம் அன்று என்று வற்புறுத்தியது

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season and its flowers fix mullai

comparisons.tenor: the heat shimmering over the waste

100.reading: The other woman says she laughs whenever she thinks of it: when the lord of the town of cool fords, where aambal stands in deep water like the plumage of the sharp-clawed heron of the rains, seized her honey-scented braids and snatched her bright bangles, and at the uproar she said, with an angry face but no anger, that she would go and tell his wife, the good man's trembling terror throbbed like the clay-smeared face of the drum the musicians play lovingly in the land of Malaiyan, giver of chariots, of great old fame, whose bow drives off the long cattle herds of enemy towns.
100.nuance: She mocks him as நன்னர் ஆளன் (the good man) and makes sure the wife's people overhear: the man who grabs her in the street shakes at the thought of his wife, so the other woman claims the upper hand. A great raider's festival drum is borrowed to measure a philanderer's fright.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தை தலைவிக்குப்பாங்காயினார் கேட்ப விறலிக்கு உடம்படச்சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the quarrel between the town lord, his wife and the other woman is the marutham situation

comparisons.tenor: the aambal of the deep ford

comparisons.vehicle: நலம் புரி முழவின் மண் ஆர் கண்ணின்

links.note: Kural 1268 wishes the king victory so that the man may join his wife and keep an evening feast for guests; Natrinai 81 is that moment reached: the king has quelled the enemy and the man hurries home to a wife whose grief was her longing to host guests.
links.teaches: Held together they show that the soldier's picture of home was a feast for guests, voiced as a wish before victory in the Kural and as a race home after it in the Natrinai, which adds that the wife's sorrow was her inability to host alone, so hospitality is a couple's act that war suspends.

links.note: In Kural 1082 the man is struck by her answering look as by a goddess with an army; in Natrinai 82 the man says he cannot bear to look at her form, which strikes his eyes like Valli joined with Murugan.
links.teaches: The Kural puts the wound in her returned glance, the Natrinai in his own looking at her beauty, and only the Natrinai can name the goddess as the hill's own Valli, so the divine attack of the Kural's abstract couplet is, in the older poem, a local deity of the land where the love happens.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 153 the girl's heart, which once took fright when the hill owl hooted, now goes out through the dark night toward him; in Natrinai 83 the friend begs the owl at the town ghat not to sound its fearful cry while they wait awake for him.
links.teaches: The owl's cry is the standard measure of the night tryst's fear, and the pair shows it split between two roles: love has carried the girl's heart past that fear, while the friend, who manages the meeting, still has to buy the owl's silence with offerings.

links.note: Kural 81 says that all of keeping a home and guarding its goods is for caring for guests and doing good; Natrinai 84 says the man leaves his wife for the waste because he cannot live a home life that fails to relieve those who come begging.
links.teaches: The Natrinai shows the cost of the Kural's rule: if a household exists to give, a household without wealth fails its purpose, so the very ideal that defines home life is what sends the husband away from home and leaves the wife to grieve.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 21 the woman refuses to believe the konrai's sign of the rains because he does not lie; in Natrinai 86 the friend calls the men righteous because they came back before the season they had named.
links.teaches: The Kuruntokai woman's faith that he keeps his word is a wager, and the Natrinai shows the wager won, with the kept promise named as அறவர், virtue, so truthfulness about the season is what the akam poets count as a husband's righteousness.

links.note: In Natrinai 86 the friend reads the flowers of the late dew and early summer as true signs that the man came before his season; in Natrinai 99 she calls the rainy-season flowers foolish, blooming for a rain that is not the season, because he has not come.
links.teaches: Read together they show that the friend's reading of the season's signs follows the man's conduct, not the signs themselves: when he keeps time the flowers are witnesses, when he does not they are fools, so the season in akam is an argument made for the woman's sake.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 201 a bat that has eaten sweet mango gulps sour nelli and hangs from the bamboo, in a poem of good news that the hill lord will come; in Natrinai 87 a bat hanging asleep on a mango only dreams of the sour nelli of a far forest, and her day of longing passes like that dream.
links.teaches: The same bat, mango and sour nelli carry fulfilment or its absence according to whether the bat eats or only dreams, matching the good news of Kuruntokai 201 and the empty day of Natrinai 87, so the poets varied one fixed image by a single verb to change its sense.

links.note: Kural 620 says those who toil on without flagging see fate's back; in Natrinai 88 the friend tells the girl not to be stricken as though by their own old deeds but to rise, go and speak to the man.
links.teaches: The Kural states for the man of affairs that effort overturns fate, and the Natrinai shows the same refusal of fate in a girl's friend inside a secret love, where the effort is speech to the man, so the rule had a domestic use, and the friend's action is an answer to the household's fatalism.

links.note: Kural 1222 pities the sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) evening and asks whether its partner is as hard-eyed (வன்கண்ணது) as hers; Natrinai 89 calls the evening sad (புன்கண் மாலை) but makes it the ally of the hard-hearted (வன்கணாளர்) who do not come. On this reading the evening is a fellow victim in one and an accomplice in the other.
links.teaches: The same two words, புன்கண் and வன்கண், are distributed differently: the Kural gives the evening its own hard partner and so makes it a sister in grief, while the Natrinai joins the evening to her own hard man, so the woman's view of the hour turns on whether she sees it as abandoned or as sent.

links.note: Both open with உள்ளார் கொல்லோ தோழி, the friend asking whether the men who crossed the waste will not think of them; Kuruntokai 16 answers with a lizard calling to its mate, Natrinai 92 with a tusker winning water for its mate and calf.
links.teaches: The formula comes with its answer, a male creature caring for its mate on the road the man has taken, and the pair shows that answer sharpened: a lizard's call only reminds, while a tusker that provides and then moves on mirrors the man who left to provide, so the friend's comfort lies in the likeness.

links.note: Kural 1137 praises womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not mount the palmyra horse; in Natrinai 94 the woman herself says that speaking out desire suits a man while womanhood makes her hold it in, and asks what kind of man he is not to know.
links.teaches: The Kural's praise of the woman's silence becomes in the Natrinai a grievance spoken by the woman under that rule, aimed at the man who is free to speak and does not, so the restraint the couplet admires is shown from inside as a constraint she resents.

links.note: Kural 1185 is built on the pointing words உவக்காண், இவக்காண்: look there, he goes; look here, the pallor spreads. Natrinai 96 points with இதுவே, உதுவே, அதுவே to the places where she met him, and ends on the pallor.
links.teaches: Both make pallor out of pointing, but the Kural points across the distance of a departure seen as it happens, while the Natrinai friend walks back through the places of meeting before an overhearing man, so pallor comes in one from the sight of leaving and in the other from memory of place, used to press for marriage.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 66 the friend says the konrai is foolish to bloom for a stray rain before the promised season; in Natrinai 99 the friend, answering the woman's own question, says the cloud itself forgot itself and the pidavam, konrai and kodal bloomed because they are foolish.
links.teaches: The Natrinai takes the Kuruntokai's single foolish tree and widens the folly to the sky and to three flowers, and places it as the answer to the woman's doubt, so the consolation grows from a remark about one tree into a whole season declared mistaken.

links.note: Purananuru 123 makes chariot-giving Malaiyan's mark, chariots given sober outnumbering the raindrops on Mullur; Natrinai 100 names him only as தேர் வண் மலையன் and borrows his musicians' drum to measure a frightened husband's trembling.
links.teaches: The akam poet can name Malaiyan by the epithet the puram poems established and rely on his fame being known, and turns it to mockery: the drum of a great giver's festivals throbs for a man afraid of his wife, so puram glory serves akam as a scale for comic smallness.

source_issues: 86 lines 1 to 3: the construction of மறவர் வேல் என விரிந்த கதுப்பின் தோல பாண்டில் ஒப்பின் பகன்றை is unclear (what spreads like spears, and what தோல பாண்டில் is); the flower similes are read loosely and the verse is marked uncertain.

89: the colophon gives the poem to the friend (தோழி தலைவிக்கு உரைத்தது) on hearing that the man is returning, but the poem addresses தோழி and complains of 'those who do not come' (வாரா வன்கணாளர்), which fits the woman as speaker; the colophon is copied as given.
90 lines 10 to 12: the construction of ஊசல் உறு தொழில் பூசல் கூட்டா and who is blamed for the girl's tears is unclear; marked uncertain.
93 lines 3 to 4 (கூலம் எல்லாம் புலம்புஉக) and 11 to 12 (முன் உயிர்க் குறியெதிர்ப்பை) are hard; the reading of her life as a pledge is tentative and the verse is marked uncertain.
98 line 2: செய்ய்ம்ம் மேவல் is garbled (a doubled ய் and ம்); the boar's epithet is read as 'wanting to wallow' without fixing the word, and the verse is marked uncertain.
84 line 1 is missing from sangamtamil.com's text and recurs as Natrinai 219 line 1; it is kept as our text gives it.
